transcript.content: Hello. I'm a psychiatrist, and I'm here to help you today. What brings you into the clinic?

I’m constantly worrying about everything—my kids, my job, money—and it feels like it never lets up. It's just gotten to the point where I feel completely overwhelmed, and I realized I need some help to get a handle on it.
How long have you been experiencing this constant, overwhelming worry? Has it been going on for at least six months, or did it start more recently?

It’s been going on pretty steadily for a little over a year now, so definitely longer than six months. It really started ramping up around the time my divorce was finalized and I took on a massive digital transformation project at work. Since then, the worry just hasn't let up.
Along with this constant worry, have you also been experiencing a persistently low or depressed mood, or a loss of interest in activities you usually enjoy?

I wouldn't say I'm depressed, but I've definitely lost the ability to enjoy things. Activities I used to love, like community soccer, traveling, live music, and hiking, are completely overshadowed now. My mind is constantly cycling through "what if" scenarios, making it impossible to relax and actually enjoy them.
Besides the constant worry and difficulty enjoying things, have you been experiencing feelings of hopelessness, worthlessness, or excessive guilt?

I wouldn't say I feel hopeless or worthless, but I definitely carry a lot of guilt. Lately, my nerves are so frayed that I end up snapping at my kids or coworkers over minor things, and I feel awful and guilty about it immediately afterward.
Do you often feel physically restless, keyed up, or notice that your muscles are constantly tense and tight?

Yes, constantly—it feels like I have a motor running inside me all the time. I'm always jiggling my leg in meetings, pacing around my apartment, and clenching my jaw. I can't even just sit and relax with my friends because of this urgent feeling that I should be doing something.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight since these feelings started, such as eating much less or more than usual?
Honestly, I haven't really noticed any significant changes in my appetite or weight since all of this started. My eating habits have stayed pretty much the same despite the stress.
Have you had any thoughts of self-harm, suicide, or felt that life is not worth living?
No, I don't have any thoughts of hurting myself or ending my life. Even though I feel extremely overwhelmed, stressed, and exhausted right now, I've never felt like life isn't worth living.
How has your sleep been since these feelings of worry started? Do you have trouble falling or staying asleep, or wake up feeling unrefreshed?

My sleep has been absolutely terrible. I lie in bed exhausted, but my brain keeps replaying work presentations and arguments with my ex, so I toss and turn for hours and constantly wake up to check my phone. The next day, I'm just dragging myself through work feeling like I didn't sleep a single wink.
Do you find it very difficult to control or stop these worries once they start, or do they feel completely out of your hands?

Yes, it feels completely out of my hands and impossible to switch off. Even when I try to tell myself to let things go, the worries just morph into another angle—like worrying that if I stop thinking about my work project for even a second, I’ll miss something huge and everything will fall apart.
Do you have any medical conditions, such as an overactive thyroid, or do you consume a lot of caffeine or other substances to help you get through the day?

No, I don't have any medical conditions like an overactive thyroid, and my health is generally fine otherwise. I also don't rely on excessive caffeine or use any other substances to get through the day, even though I'm completely exhausted.

opening_question.question: Hello. I'm a psychiatrist, and I'm here to help you today. What brings you into the clinic?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (ICD-10 F41.1). They present with generalized, persistent, and uncontrollable worry about multiple everyday domains (work, family, finances) lasting for over a year (well exceeding the 6-month threshold). This is accompanied by prominent physical and psychological symptoms of anxiety, including motor restlessness (pacing, leg jiggling), muscle tension (jaw clenching), irritability (snapping at others), chronic fatigue, and severe sleep disturbance (insomnia). Other conditions, such as a primary depressive episode or substance-induced anxiety, have been ruled out.
